extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator; polite society and potential contributors (artisans, tradesmen, gentlemen, and general literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for contributors to The Spectator and for polite social behaviour: what kinds of matter to submit, stylistic cautions for correspondents, and standards of etiquette and charity promoted in the periodical's essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require provenance for reports of scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports to our disadvantage should not be credited if advanced without a Person who can say whence he had it, or which is attested by one who forgot who told him it, or who had it from one of so little Consideration that he did not then think it worth his Notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (From Cicero quoted.) The Spectator recommends that hearsay lacking clear origin, or supported only by forgetful/insignificant witnesses, be treated as too slight to damage a person's honour. When an ill report can be traced to such sources it often vanishes; editors/readers should demand identifiable testimony before accepting scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not receive or propagate scandal without examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever receives Impressions to the Disadvantage of others without Examination, is to be had in no other Credit for Intelligence than this good Lady Bluemantle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the anecdote of Lady Bluemantle (a town's ubiquitous gossip who repeats matters without knowing authorship). The Spectator condemns the temper that delights only in lamentation and urges readers not to be scandal-bearers: examine, verify, and avoid taking pleasure in others' misfortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite and value practical, useful contributions from all ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper will consist also of all Things which may be necessary or useful to any Part of Society, and the mechanick Arts should have their Place as well as the Liberal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor invites correspondents from ‘the late noble Inventor of the Longitude’ to ‘the humble Author of Strops for Razors.’ Practical histories (e.g., of trades, shops, stock movements, methods of gain, husbandry, thrift) are explicitly welcomed because they serve a greater number of people than purely literary topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record concrete histories and practical particulars (business and domestic)
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be of great Use if we had an exact History of the Successes of every great Shop within the City-Walls, what Tracts of Land have been purchased by a constant Attendance within a Walk of thirty Foot...The Industry of the Female World is not to be unobserved: She to whose Household Virtues it is owing, that Men do Honour to her Husband, should be recorded with Veneration; she who had wasted his Labours, with Infamy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages submissions that give exact, instructive details about commercial success, household management, and domestic virtue/vice so readers (apprentices, traders, householders) can learn practical lessons — both positive and cautionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid technical terms and jargon unfamiliar to general readers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to caution [correspondents] only against using Terms of Art, and describing Things that are familiar to them in Words unknown to their Readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondents are warned that describing trade- or profession-specific matters using specialized vocabulary will make their accounts unintelligible; write plainly for a broad readership to have the intended practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share conversational turns; do not monopolize discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an impertinent and unreasonable Fault in Conversation, for one Man to take up all the Discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies both to social behaviour and, by analogy, to publication: the paper's editor notes the danger of dominating conversation and invites contributions so other able persons may have opportunity to oblige mankind with their thoughts (i.e., give space to diverse voices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polite-company etiquette: moderation, dress, and behaviour rules
rubrics_metrics.description: No one is to appear in the publick Rooms undressed, or enter abruptly into each other's Apartment without intimation...they have but one Offender in ten Days Time been sent into the Infirmary, and that was for throwing away his Cards at Whist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples of offences and corrective measures: avoid undress in public rooms, give notice before entering others' apartments, practise moderation in gestures and gaming, abstain from disruptive behaviour (swearing, stamping, throwing cards). The ‘Infirmary’ is used as a humorous institutional sanction for breaches of decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control affective displays in mixed company (married persons' behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: The strange Freedoms some ill-bred married People take in Company: The unseasonable Fondness of some Husbands, and the ill-timed Tenderness of some Wives...I beg you would be pleased to take Notice of a very great Indecency...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public displays of excessive intimacy or private domestic topics in mixed company are improper; modesty and restraint are expected in polite assemblies. The Spectator asks for censure/correction of such misbehaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be discerning and charitable: give to real objects of charity, punish impostors
rubrics_metrics.description: They ought to be taken Care of in this Condition, either by the Beadle or the Magistrate...If we have nothing else for our Money, let us have more Invention to be cheated with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While urging compassion for the visibly needy (disabled sailors, soldiers), the essay also requests civic mechanisms to distinguish impostors from true beggars (use officers to hear constant beggars' distress). Charity should not be abandoned, but societal oversight is needed to prevent widespread imposture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject prejudice and petty faction; foster generous emulation
rubrics_metrics.description: General Charges against Bodies of Men is the Fault I am writing against...By such early Corrections of Vanity, while Boys are growing into Men, they will gradually learn not to censure superficially; but imbibe those Principles of general Kindness and Humanity...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An essay from Oxford urges citizens (and educators) to avoid irrational contempt for other nations, parishes, professions, or colleges; do not foster vain exclusivity or debase others to elevate one’s own group. Instead, present varied exemplary figures to youth so ambition and honest emulation — not slavish imitation or petty envy — are cultivated.
